\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

The problem of finding vertex-disjoint paths between fixed pairs of
vertices of a given graph has been well-studied in the last fifty
years. It is \textsc{NP}-complete on directed
graphs~\cite{FORTUNE1980111}, and polynomial on undirected
graphs~\cite{DBLP:journals/dm/Seymour80,DBLP:journals/jacm/Shiloach80,DBLP:journals/ejc/Thomassen80}.

Many variations of this problem exist, such as optimisation
versions~\cite{https://doi.org/10.1002/net.3230140209}, acyclic
case~\cite{DBLP:journals/jacm/PerlS78}, etc. Here, we focus on the
following one: given vertices $s_1,t_1,s_2,t_2$ in a simple undirected
graph, find vertex-disjoint paths respectively from $s_1$ to $t_1$ and
from $s_2$ to $t_2$. If $s_1=s_2$ or $t_1=t_2$, then this problem is
solved by Menger's theorem: say $s_1=s_2$; the two paths exist if and
only if every vertex separator between $s_1$ and $\{t_1,t_2\}$ has at
least two elements. Various methods relating to flow networks exist to
solve such a problem. The difficulty arises when $s_1\neq s_2$ and
$t_1\neq t_2$. The corresponding algorithmic problem is usually called
the ``two disjoint paths'' problem. Menger's theorem would apply to
find vertex-disjoint paths between $\{s_1,s_2\}$ and $\{t_1,t_2\}$,
but requiring $s_1$-$t_1$ and $s_2$-$t_2$ paths makes the problem
harder.

Since the seminal works
in~\cite{DBLP:journals/dm/Seymour80,DBLP:journals/jacm/Shiloach80,DBLP:journals/ejc/Thomassen80},
many efficient algorithms have been given: we find respectively
in~\cite{DBLP:journals/siamcomp/KhullerMV92,gustedt,DBLP:journals/mst/Tholey06}
algorithms running in $O(n^2)$, $O(n+m\log n)$, and
$O(n+m\alpha(m,n))$ where $n$ and $m$ are respectively the vertex and
edge number of the graph, and $\alpha$ is the two parameters variant
of the inverse of the Ackermann function. All are based on improving
the $O(nm)$ algorithm by
Shiloach~\cite{DBLP:journals/jacm/Shiloach80}. The latter relies on a
sequence of six reductions, three of which involve previous works:
instances can be reduced to the $3$-connected case (e.g. using the
algorithm from~\cite{doi:10.1137/0202012} to decompose a graph into
its triconnected components), and even the $3$-connected non-planar
case~\cite{DBLP:journals/jacm/PerlS78}, both in $O(n+m)$ time. By
Kuratowksi's Theorem the resulting instance contains a topological
$K_{3,3}$ or $K_5$. Another reduction allows one to assume that the
instance does not contain a
$K_5$~\cite{10.1215/S0012-7094-68-03523-0}.

From a structural point of view, the characterisation of graphs
avoiding vertex-disjoint paths between two fixed pairs of vertices is
often called the two paths theorem. It states that the edge-maximal
such graphs are the \emph{webs}. It was first introduced
in~\cite{DBLP:journals/ejc/Thomassen80,DBLP:journals/dm/Seymour80}.

We provide a new proof of this theorem, and we use it to design a
simple $O(nm)$ algorithm for a slight generalisation of the two
disjoint paths problem. Our algorithm departs from the method of
Shiloach in that no reductions are required: it is a simple recursive
algorithm and except for a search algorithm (e.g. depth-first or
bread-first), it is self-contained.

We start by fixing the notations and conventions that we use for
graphs, before introducing the mains definitions more formally.

\subsection{Graph conventions}
We only consider simple and undirected graphs, with the following
conventions. Given a graph $G$, we write $V(G)$ for its set of
\emph{vertices} and $E(G)$ for its set of \emph{edges}---two-elements
sets of vertices. We often use a graph to denote its underlying set of
vertices, thus writting $G$ for $V(G)$; similarly, we often write $x$
for the singleton set $\{x\}$. We note $n=|V(G)|$ the \emph{order} of
$G$ and $m=|E(G)|$ the \emph{size} of $G$. If $G'$ is another graph,
then $G\uplus G'$ is the \emph{disjoint union} of $G$ with $G'$.
%
Given $V\subseteq V(G)$ a subset of vertices, we note $G[V]$ for the
\emph{subgraph of $G$ induced by $V$}, and $G-V$ for the graph $G$
where all vertices of $V$ and incident edges have been removed. An
\emph{edge subgraph} of a graph $G$ is a graph $H$ with $V(H)=V(G)$
and $E(H)\subseteq E(G)$.
%
If $F$ is a set of edges on $V(G)$ then $G+F$ is the graph obtained
from $G$ by adding the edges in $F$. Given $R$ an equivalence relation
between vertices of $G$, $G/R$ denotes the graph obtained by
identifying vertices in each equivalence classes---when $R$ is not
already an equivalence relation, we implicitly consider its
equivalence closure.
%
A \emph{path} $P$ is a sequence of adjacent vertices; it is an
\emph{induced path} if it is induced as a subgraph. Given a path
$P=x_1\dots x_k$, the \emph{interior} of $P$ is
$\mathring{P}=x_2\dots x_{k-1}$, and the \emph{reversal} of $P$ is
$\overline{P}=x_k\dots x_1$. Given a second path $Q=y_1\dots y_r$
with, say, $x_i=y_j$, we note $Px_iQ$ for the path from $x_1$ to $y_r$
induced by $x_1\dots x_iy_{j+1}\dots y_r$. If $x_k=y_1$, we simply
note $PQ$ for $Px_kQ$. If $x_1=y_r$ and $x_s\neq y_t$ whenever $1<s<k$
and $1<t<r$ then $PQ$ denotes the cycle $x_1\dots x_ky_2\dots y_r$.

Given two sets $H,K$ of vertices, a path $P=x_1\dots x_k$ is an
\emph{$H$-$K$ path} if $x_1\in H$, $x_k\in K$, and
$x_i\not\in H\cup K$ for all $1<i<k$. When $H=K$ we simply say that
$P$ is an \emph{$H$-path}. A vertex $x$ is \emph{$H$-connected to $K$}
when there is an $x$-$K$ path which is also a
$(\{x\}\cup K\cup H)$-path. In this work, \emph{disjoint paths} always
means vertex-disjoint paths.

Finally, a subset $X$ of vertices \emph{separates} a vertex $x$ from a
vertex $y$ when all $x$-$y$ paths contain a vertex of $X$.

\subsection{Standard two paths theorem}

A graph is \emph{$2$-linked} if for all pairwise distinct vertices
$s_1,t_1,s_2,t_2$, there are two disjoint paths, respectively from
$s_1$ to $t_1$ and from $s_2$ to $t_2$.
%
A \emph{rib} is a planar graph such that in one of its plane
embeddings, the outer face is a cycle of length four, all inner faces
are triangles, and all triangles are faces. A \emph{web} is a graph
constructed from a rib $R$ by adding one clique $C_T$ per triangle $T$
in $R$, making vertices of $C_T$ adjacent to exactly the vertices of
$T$.
\begin{restatable}[Two paths theorem%
~\cite{DBLP:journals/ejc/Thomassen80,DBLP:journals/dm/Seymour80}]{theorem}{theomain}%
  \label{theo:main}%
  The edge-maximal graphs amongst the ones which are not $2$-linked are exactly the webs.
\end{restatable}
%
In~\cite{DBLP:journals/ejc/Thomassen80}, Thomassen relies on
Kuratowski's theorem after reducing the problem along small
separators. Independently~\cite{DBLP:journals/dm/Seymour80}, Seymour
sketched a proof relying on reducing the problem to the $2$-connected
case followed by a clever combinatorial analysis of the graph's
separators. Both proofs use Menger's theorem.

\subsection{Generalised two paths theorem}

Our proof departs from such connectivity reduction strategies and uses
neither Kuratowski's nor Menger's theorems. Instead we use graph
operations generating webs. Webs as defined above are not flexible
enough to carry such a study. Hence we generalise their definition:
\begin{definition}
  Given $k\ge 3$, a \emph{$k$-rib} is a planar graph such that in
  one of its plane embeddings, the outer face is a
  $k$-cycle called its \emph{frame}, all inner faces
  are triangles, and all triangles are faces.

  A \emph{$k$-web} is a graph constructed from
  a $k$-rib $R$ by adding one clique $C_T$ per triangle $T$ of $R$,
  making vertices of $C_T$ adjacent to exactly the vertices of $T$.
  We call \emph{rib vertices} the vertices of a web that are vertices of its rib, and \emph{clique vertices} the vertices from the added cliques.
\end{definition}

In the sequel, when the size of the frame is not relevant, we often
simply call ribs and webs the graphs from this generalised definition,
. Note that in the litterature ribs are often called
``\emph{near-triangulations of the plane}''~\cite{TUTTE1980105}, and webs are
exactly the $4$-webs.

\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics{web_examples.pdf}
  \caption{Some examples of webs and ribs: dotted red vertices and
    edges are clique vertices and edges, while plain black ones are
    rib vertices and edges. The black dashed edge in the bottom right
    web is discussed in Section~\ref{sec:web_composition}. The ribs of
    the webs on the top line are actually the only ribs of order $3$,
    $4$, and $5$.}
  \label{fig:web_examples}
\end{figure}
Some examples of webs and ribs are given in Figure~\ref{fig:web_examples}. The rib
of the web on the top left corner actually is the only $3$-rib:
\begin{proposition}
  \label{prop:3_webs}
  A $3$-rib is just a triangle; a $3$-web is just a clique.
\end{proposition}

The statement of the two paths theorem needs to be adapted to
$k$-webs. Instead of looking for disjoint paths between two pairs of
vertices, we look for disjoint paths \emph{crossing} a given tuple (of
length $k$):
\begin{definition}
  Given $k\geq 3$, a \emph{crossing} of a tuple $T=(x_1,\dots,x_k)$ of
  pairwise distinct vertices is a pair of disjoint $T$-paths, from
  $x_i$ to $x_j$ and $x_r$ to $x_s$ respectively, such that
  $i<r<j<s$. A tuple $T$ is \emph{crossed} if it admits a crossing, it
  is \emph{crossless} otherwise; if $T$ is crossless and the addition
  of any edge to the graph generates a crossing, then the graph is
  \emph{maximally crossless for $T$}.
\end{definition}
Two examples of crossings are given in Figure~\ref{fig:crossings};
they are crossings in the bottom ribs of Figure~\ref{fig:web_examples}
but for a tuple different from their frames.
\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics{crossing_examples.pdf}
  \caption{Two examples of crossings (the red dashed paths) for some cycles (the blue dotted cycles).}
  \label{fig:crossings}
\end{figure}

Note that a graph is $2$-linked precisely when all tuples of four
distinct vertices are crossed. Moreover, a tuple of length three
cannot be crossed, so that a graph is maximally crossless for a tuple
of length three if and only if it is edge maximal, thus a clique. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:3_webs} this shows that maximally crossless
graphs for tuples $T$ of three vertices are precisely $3$-webs with
frame $T$. In general and instead of Theorem~\ref{theo:main} we prove
the following:
\begin{restatable}[Generalised two paths theorem]{theorem}{theomaintwo}%
  \label{theo:main_2}%
  The maximally crossless graphs for a tuple $T$ are the webs with frame $T$.
\end{restatable}
This statement when $|T|=4$ is equivalent to that of Theorem~\ref{theo:main}.
It moreover follows that in a graph with a given tuple $T$, either $T$ is crossed or the graph embeds in a web with frame $T$.

The motivation for our generalisation from $4$-webs to $k$-webs is
that those can be characterised inductively. As will be shown in
Section~\ref{sec:webs}, webs are inductively generated from cliques by
successive \emph{parallel compositions}. This operation consists in
taking the disjoint union of two webs followed by the pairwise
identification of vertices along some well-chosen subpaths of their
frames. The issue with restricting with $4$-webs is that these are not
stable under parallel composition.


The structural insights given by our proof allow for the design of a $O(nm)$ algorithm to:
\begin{enumerate}
\item decide whether a given tuple $T$ is crossed in a graph,
\item if so, compute a crossing of $T$,
\item otherwise, compute an embedding of the input graph in a web with frame $T$.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Outline}

We study webs in Section~\ref{sec:webs}. We show that they can be generated inductively, and eventually, that they are maximally crossless. This is the easy implication of the two paths theorem.
The other implication is the difficult one in the works of Thomassen~\cite{DBLP:journals/ejc/Thomassen80} and Seymour~\cite{DBLP:journals/dm/Seymour80}; we prove it in Section~\ref{sec:proof_theomain}. Thanks to our generalisation, we provide a direct proof, by induction. We present our algorithm for the two disjoint paths problem in Section~\ref{sec:algorithm}; unsurprisingly, its recursive structure follows the inductive structure of our proof.

\section{Webs}
\label{sec:webs}

An immediate yet important observation that we use throughout the
paper is that in a web, the intersection with the rib of a path whose
ends are on the rib yields an induced path. (And conversely, induced
paths whose ends are on the rib must be entirely on the rib.) Indeed,
if such a path uses a clique vertex $u$, then we can consider the
longest subpath $P$ of it containing $u$ and only clique vertices. Its
ends are on a triangle of the rib whose clique vertices contain all
the inner vertices of $P$. In particular $P$ can be replaced by an
edge of the triangle:
\begin{center}
  \includegraphics{induced_paths.pdf}
\end{center}
(In this figure the green triangular shape in the center of the
triangle represents all the clique vertices of the triangle.)

The argument from~\cite{DBLP:journals/ejc/Thomassen80}, proving that frames
of $4$-webs are not $2$-linked, generalises easily:
\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:frame_crossless}
  Frames of webs are crossless.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  Suppose by contradiction that the frame of a web is crossed.  The
  union of the frame and the paths from the crossing gives a
  topological $K_4$. By intersecting with the rib, we can assume these
  paths are induced in the rib, which gives a topological $K_4$ in the
  rib. Considering a planar embedding of it in which the frame bounds
  the outer face, this would give an outerplanar plane embedding of
  $K_4$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Web compositions}
\label{sec:web_composition}

A natural way of composing webs consists is taking their disjoint
union and then identifying two edges from their respective frames. For
example, the rib in the bottom right corner of
Figure~\ref{fig:web_examples} can be obtained by such an operation
(the edge resulting from the identification being the black dashed one),
whereas the rib in the bottom left corner of this figure cannot. Such
an operation always produces webs: plane embeddings can be composed in
this way, all triangles remain faces and all inner faces will remain
triangles. If the identified edges are denoted $e$ and $e'$ and
the frames of the composed webs are respectively $Pe$ and $P'e'$,
then the resulting web has frame $PP'$.

We generalise this operation to identify subpaths of frames instead of
single edges. If $P=x_1\dots x_l$ and $P'=x'_1\dots x'_l$ are
non-empty paths of two graphs $G$ and $H$, respectively, we define the
\emph{parallel composition} of $G$ with $H$ along $P$ and $P'$ as
\[
  (G\uplus H)/\{(x_1,x_1'),\dots,(x_l,x_l')\}
\]
When $P=P'$ we simply talk of \emph{parallel composition along
  $P$}. In the particular case presented above, in which $P$ and $P'$
are reduced to one edge each, we talk of \emph{edge composition}.

The issue is that taking a parallel composition of two webs along
subpaths of their frames does not always give a web (although this is
true for edge compositions, as explained above). In the following
example, the red edges $xz$ and $uw$ become parallel when merging the
plane embeddings of the two ribs on the left hand-side by identifying
the paths $xyz$ and $uvw$. We are working with simple graphs, so in
the parallel composition of the two ribs along these paths, the two
parallel dashed edges on the right hand-side become one edge $e$. In a
plane embedding of the parallel composition, $e$ can be shared by only
two triangles: one of the three triangles containing it cannot be a
face, and the resulting graph is not a rib, and not a web
either.\medskip
\begin{center}
  \includegraphics{bad_parallel_composition.pdf}
\end{center}
To ensure parallel compositions send webs to webs, the identified
subpaths of their frames must be carefuly chosen. In fact, it suffices
that those subpaths are induced: given two webs $G,H$ with induced
subpaths $P$ and $P'$ of their respective frames and of the same
length, we call \emph{web composition} of $G$ with $H$ along $P$ and
$P'$ the parallel composition of $G$ with $H$ along $P$ and $P'$.
\begin{proposition}
  \label{prop:web_stability}
  Webs are stable under web composition.

  More precisely, the parallel composition along $P$ and $P'$ of two
  webs $G$ and $H$ with respective frames $P_GP$ and $P_HP'$ is a web
  with frame $P_GP_H$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
  Let $G,H$ be two webs with respective frames $C_G$ and $C_H$ and let
  $P$ and $P'$ be induced paths of same length, such that $C_G=P_GP$
  and $C_H=P_HP'$.

  Consider the ribs $R_G$ and $R_H$ of $G$ and $H$ as well as plane
  embeddings of both in which $C_G$ and $C_H$ bound the outer faces,
  all inner faces are triangles, and all triangles faces. In
  particular, $P$ and $P'$ are both on the outer faces.

  The web composition $R$ of $R_G$ and $R_H$ along $P$ and $P'$ is
  again a rib. Indeed, any planar graph admits a plane embedding with
  its outer face being exactly in a given prescribed polygon of the
  plane (see \cite{article/lms/tutte60}). Choosing the right polygons
  we can build a plane embedding of $R$. The only issue could be that
  some edges between vertices of $P$ and $P'$ were drawn twice, once
  as an edge of $R_G$ and once as an edge of $R_H$. Having assumed
  that $P$ and $P'$ are induced, this cannot be. This also shows that
  triangles of $G$ and $H$ are distinct in $R$. Hence, adding back the
  clique vertices of $G$ and $H$ on their respective triangles we get
  a web, proving that the web composition of $G$ with $H$ along $P$
  and $P'$ is a web with rib $R$ and frame $P_GP_H$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Web decompositions}

We prove below that all webs can be inductively generated from cliques
via web compositions.  Before doing so, we prove an important
property. If we do not use connectivity reduction proof schemes or
Menger's theorem, we do prove one connectivity result on webs. It
shows how edge compositions of webs are essential to connectivity of
webs up-to frames.
\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:connectivity_lemma_webs}
  Given vertices $x,y$ in a web with frame $C$, either $x$ is
  $C$-connected to $y$, or there is a pair of vertices $c,c'\in C\backslash\{x,y\}$
  separating $x$ from $y$ and such that the web can be expressed as
  the edge composition of two webs along $cc'$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  It is sufficient to prove the statement for ribs. Indeed, except
  perhaps for its ends, we have seen that induced paths in webs
  are paths in their ribs.

  Consider a rib $R$ with frame $C$ in which two vertices $x$ and $y$
  are not $C$-connected. We prove that $R$ is given as the edge
  composition of two ribs along some edge $cc'$ for $c,c'\in C\backslash\{x,y\}$
  with $x$ and $y$ being separated by $\{c,c'\}$.

  Obviously ribs are connected. Hence some vertices $c_x$ and $c_y$ of
  $C$ must respectively be $C$-connected to $x$ and $y$. If this is
  the only such vertex for $x$ or $y$ then $\{c_x,c_y\}$ separates $x$
  from $y$. Otherwise there are vertices $c_x'$ and $c_y'$
  respectively distinct from $c_x$ and $c_y$ and $C$-connected to $x$
  and $y$ respectively. The $C$-paths from $c_x$ to $x$ and from $x$
  to $c_x'$ induce some $C$-path from $c_x$ to $c_x'$, and similarly
  we get some $C$-path from $c_y$ to $c_y'$. By
  Lemma~\ref{lem:frame_crossless}, $C$ is not crossed in $R$, so that
  these paths cannot form a crossing of $C$.

  Note $C=c_1\dots c_kc_1$. W.l.o.g. we can assume that $c_x=c_i$,
  $c_x'=c_j$ for $i<j$, and whenever $c_t$ is $C$-connected to $y$,
  then $i\le t\le j$. Assume $i$ and $j$ are respectively the maximum
  and minimum indices as such. In particular there is no index $t$
  with $i<t<j$ such that $c_t$ is $C$-connected to $x$, no index $t$
  with $t< i$ or $t> j$ such that $c_t$ is $C$-connected to $y$ and
  $y$ is $C$-connected to both $c_i$ and $c_j$. This gives that
  $x,y\notin\{c_i,c_j\}$.

  We prove that $\{c_i,c_j\}$ separates $x$ from $y$. If it wasn't the
  case, then there would be a $C$-path from $x$ to $c_t$ with $i<t<j$
  or a $C$-path from $y$ to $c_t$ with $t<i$ or $t>j$, both
  consequences being contradictions.

  We set $c=c_i$ and $c'=c_j$.
  Consider a plane embedding of $R$ whose outer face is bounded by
  $C$, all inner faces being triangles, and all triangles being faces.
  As $\{c,c'\}$ is a separator, this embedding must have the shape
  shown below. Without being too formal on the manipulation of such
  embeddings, the green area must correspond to an inner face of the
  embedding, meaning a triangle. This face being incident to both
  $c$ and $c'$, that implies that $cc'$ is an edge of
  $R$.
  \medskip

  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics{connectivity_lemma.pdf}
  \end{center}
  The fact that $R$ is given by an edge composition of two ribs
  along $cc'$ is then direct by looking at the inner faces and triangles
  of $H$ and $K$.
\end{proof}
\begin{remark}
  \label{rem:connectivity_lemma_webs}
  A global version of the above lemma would be: ``in a web, either all
  pairs of vertices are $C$-connected, or the web is the edge
  composition of two webs, one statement excluding the other''. A
  third version can be extracted from the proof. Instead of looking at
  the $C$-connectedness between two vertices, we look at a given
  vertex $x$ and a subpath $P$ of $C$: either $P$ is
  $C$-connected to $x$ or there are vertices $c,c'$ of $C-P$
  separating $x$ from $P$ and such that $G$ is given as an edge
  composition of two webs along $cc'$.
\end{remark}
\begin{corollary}
  \label{corol:path_web}
  In a web whose frame $C$ has length at least four, there is a
  $C$-path whose ends are non-consecutive vertices of $C$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
  As $|C|\ge 4$, consider two non-consecutive vertices $c,c'$ of
  $C$. If $c$ is $C$-connected to $c'$ then this provides a $C$-path
  whose ends are non-consecutive vertices of $C$.  Otherwise, by
  Lemma~\ref{lem:connectivity_lemma_webs}, the web is given as an
  edge composition along some edge $uu'$ between vertices of $C$. This
  edge provides a $C$-path whose ends are non-consecutive vertices of
  $C$ as $\{u,u'\}$ separates $c$ from $c'$.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}
  \label{prop:generating_webs_parallel}
  Every web whose frame has length at least four is a web composition.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
  Let $G$ be a web with rib $R$ and frame $C$ with $|C|\geq 4$.  By
  Corollary~\ref{corol:path_web} there is a $C$-path $P$ whose ends
  are non-consecutive vertices of $C$. We can assume w.l.o.g. that $P$
  is an induced path, i.e., a path in $R$.  Considering a plane
  embedding of the latter, the path $P$ separates $R$ into two planar
  graphs whose outer faces are bounded by the two cycles induced by
  $C$ and $P$, all their faces are faces of $R$ and hence triangles,
  and all their triangles are triangles of $R$ and hence faces: those
  two planar graphs are ribs. Adding back the cliques vertices of $G$
  on their respective triangles, the resulting pair of webs generate
  $G$ by taking their web composition along $P$.
\end{proof}

Alltogether, Propositions~\ref{prop:3_webs},~\ref{prop:web_stability},
and~\ref{prop:generating_webs_parallel} show that the webs are
precisely the graphs obtained by repeated web compositions, starting
from cliques (whose frames are any triangle).

\subsection{Maximality}

We have seen that frames of webs are crossless in Lemma~\ref{lem:frame_crossless}. Using the previous inductive characterisation of webs, we can easily show that they are actually maximally crossless, which is the first half of our main theorem.
\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:web_are_edge_maximal}
  Every web is maximally crossless for its frame.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  We reason by induction on the order of the considered web. Webs with
  frame of length three being cliques by
  Proposition~\ref{prop:3_webs}, they are edge-maximal for any
  property. Thus, let $G$ be a web with frame $C$ of length at least
  four. By Proposition~\ref{prop:generating_webs_parallel}, $G$ is the
  web composition of two webs $H$ and $K$ along some induced $C$-path
  $P$ of $G$. Let $C_H$ and $C_K$ be the frames of $H$ and $K$,
  respectively. By induction hypothesis, $H$ and $K$ are maximally
  crossless for $C_H$ and $C_K$, respectively.

  Note that as $P$ is induced in both $H$ and $K$, these webs cannot
  be expressed as some edge composition along some edge between
  non-consecutive vertices of $P$. By the last version of
  Lemma~\ref{lem:connectivity_lemma_webs} as given in
  Remark~\ref{rem:connectivity_lemma_webs}, this implies that all
  vertices of $H$ are $C_H$-connected to $C_H-P$ in $H$, and
  similarly for $K$.

  Let $e$ be some edge on $V(G)$ that is not in $G$. We prove that $C$
  is crossed in $G+e$.

  Assume the two ends of $e=xy$ are respectively in $H-P$ and $K-P$.
  As $x$ is $C_H$-connected to $C_H-P$ in $H$ and $y$ is
  $C_K$-connected to $C_K-P$ in $K$, we can assume we have an
  $x$-$(C_H-P)$ (resp. $y$-$(C_K-P)$) path $P_x$ in $H$ (resp.
  $P_y$ in $K$) disjoint from $P$. The pair $(P_xeP_y,P)$ is a
  crossing of $C$ in $G+e$.

  Otherwise $e$ has both its ends in either $H$ or $K$, say in $H$. By
  induction hypothesis, let $(P_1,P_2)$ be a crossing of $C_H$ in
  $H+e$. We reason by case analysis depending on which ends of $P_1$
  and $P_2$ are on $P$.  Up-to symmetries between $P_1$ and $P_2$,
  there are five cases, represented in Figure~\ref{fig:five_cases}
  with the shape of the crossing of $C$ we build in $G+e$. The first
  three in which both $P_1$ and $P_2$ have at least one end not on $P$
  are self-explanatory and just require the use of $P$ to extend $P_1$
  and/or $P_2$ to form a crossing of $C$ in $G+e$. The last two
  require a bit more work in order to prove the existence of the added
  dashed purple paths.
  \begin{figure}
    \centering
    \includegraphics{five_cases.pdf}
    \caption{At the top, the five possible shapes of crossings in
      subwebs w.r.t. $P$ and $C$. At the bottom, the five shapes of
      the deduced crossings in whole graph.}
    \label{fig:five_cases}
  \end{figure}

  In the fourth case, if the end of $P_1$ which is on $P$ is noted
  $z$, then, as already shown, $z$ is $C_K$-connected to $C_K-P$ in
  $K$, providing a path $P'$. If $P_2$'s ends are $x$ and $y$, then
  $(PxP_2yP,P_1zP')$ is a crossing of $C$ in $G+e$.

  In the fifth case, we first note that $P_1$ and $P_2$ cannot be
  reduced to edges as $P$ is induced. All their inner vertices being
  $C_H$-connected to $C_H-P$, consider an associated path $P'$.
  Up-to replacing $P'$ by its portion starting on the last vertex of
  in either $P_1$ or $P_2$, we get, say, a
  $(C_H-P)$-$\mathring{P_1}$ path inner disjoint with $P_1$, $P_2$,
  and $C_H$. Note it $P'$ with $u$ its end on $P_1$. If $z$ is the end
  of $P_1$ that is surrounded by $P_2$'s ends on $P$, then just as
  above we get a $z$-$(C_K-P)$ path $P''$ in $K$ that is inner
  disjoint with $C_K$. If $P_2$'s ends are $x$ and $y$ then
  $(P'uP_1zP'',PxP_2yP)$ is a crossing of $C$ in $G+e$.
\end{proof}

\section{Proving the two paths theorem}
\label{sec:proof_theomain}

We now prove the direct implication of the two paths theorem, which is
the difficult one in the litterature.

Observe that edges of shape $x_tx_{t+1}$ and $x_kx_1$ cannot be used
in crossings of a tuple $T=x_1,\dots,x_k$. Said otherwise, if $F$ is
the set of such edges, then $T$ is crossed in a graph $G$ iff it is
crossed in $G+F$. Up-to adding these edges, we will usually assume
that $T$ is in fact a cycle $C=x_1\dots x_kx_1$ and talk of crossings
for cycles.

\begin{lemma}
  Every graph which is maximally crossless for a cycle $C$ is a web
  with frame $C$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  Let $G$ be a maximally crossless graph for a cycle $C$.
  We proceed by induction on $|G|$.

  We perform case analysis on whether all pairs of distinct vertices
  of $C$ are $C$-connected or not.

  \textbf{1/ There are two vertices $x$ and $x'$ of $C$ which are not $C$-connected.}\\
  Figure~\ref{fig:first_3_1} serves as an illustration of the following reasoning.

  Note $y$ and $z$ for the two neighbours of $x$ on $C$. Trivially,
  $x,y,z$ are all $C$-connected to $x$. As $x$ is not $C$-connected to
  $x'$, we can consider $P'$ the longest path portion of $C$ containing
  $x'$ whose inner vertices are all not $C$-connected to $x$.
  Let $P$ be the path of $C$
  such that $C=PP'$. We prove that if $u$ and $v$ are inner
  respectively in $P$ and $P'$ then they are not $C$-connected. By
  definition inner vertices of $P'$ are not $C$-connected to $x$, so
  assume $u\neq x$. By contradiction let $Q$ be a $u$-$v$ path inner
  disjoint from $C$. Let $w$ be the endpoint of $P$ such that $u$ is
  inner in $wPx$, and let $w'$ be the other end of $P$. By minimality
  of $P$, there is an $x$-$w$ path $R$ inner disjoint from $C$. If $Q$
  and $R$ were not disjoint, then they would induce an $x$-$v$ path
  inner disjoint from $C$, a contradiction. Otherwise, $(Q,R)$ is a
  crossing of $C$ in $G$, a contradiction.
  \begin{figure}
    \centering
    \includegraphics{u_v_non_accessible.pdf}
    \caption{The outer cycle is $C$, and $P$ and $P'$ are the two
      distinct $w$-$w'$ paths on $C$.}
    \label{fig:first_3_1}
  \end{figure}

  We have just shown that $\{w,w'\}$ separates $C$ in $G$ in at least
  two components respectively containing $P$ and $P'$. In particular
  the edge $ww'$ cannot be used to produce a crossing of $C$ in
  $G$. By maximality of $G$, $ww'\in E(G)$, and we can see $G$ as
  given by the edge composition of two graphs along $ww'$ respectively
  containing $P$ and $P'$. Quite directly, these two graphs are
  maximally crossless for $Pww'$ and $P'ww'$, respectively. By
  induction hypothesis they are webs and, by
  Proposition~\ref{prop:web_stability}, $G$ is a web.

  \textbf{2/ All pairs of distinct vertices of $C$ are $C$-connected.}\\
  Take consecutive vertices $x,y,z$ on $C$ with an
  $x$-$z$ path $P$ inner disjoint from $C$. For such paths $P$ we note
  $\mathcal{C}_C^P$ the component of $C-x-y-z$ in $G-P$. We assume
  that $P$ is minimal with regard to the measure
  \[
    \mu(P)=(|G|-|\mathcal{C}_C^P|,|P|)
  \]
  where the order on $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ is the lexicographic product of
  the usual order $<$. Said otherwise we choose $P$ to maximise the order
  of the component of $G-P$ containing $C-x-y-z$ while minimising the
  length of $P$. In particular, $P$ is induced.

  Take $u$ an inner vertex of $P$. We prove that
  $u$ is $C\cup P$-connected to $C-x-y-z$. By contradiction
  assume not. Let $v,w\in P$ be such that $vPw$ contains $u$ as an
  inner vertex and is the longest subpath of $P$ whose inner vertices
  are all not $C\cup P$-connected to $C-x-y-z$. As $P$ is induced
  and as $vPw$ contains at least $u$ as an inner vertex, $G$ does not
  contain $vw$.

  Consider $G+vw$. By maximality of $G$, $C$ is crossed in $G+vw$. Let
  $(P_1,P_2)$ be a crossing of $C$ in $G+vw$, with, say,
  $vw\in E(P_1)$. The path $P_2$ must contain some inner vertex of
  $vPw$ as otherwise $(P_2,P_1vPwP_1)$ would be a crossing of $C$ in
  $G$.

  One end of $P_2$ at least must be on $C-y$. W.l.o.g, assume this is
  the case of its last vertex. Let $s$ be the last vertex in $vPw$
  seen by $P_2$. As the last vertex of $P_2$ is on $C-y$ and as $s$ is
  not $C\cup P$-connected to $(C-x-y-z)$, $sP_2$ must either
  intersect $C\cup P$ at one of its inner vertex $t$ or its last
  vertex is $x$ or $z$. In the first case, as $P_2$ is a $C$-path, we actually have $t\in V(P)$. In any case, there is a vertex
  $t$ of $sP_2$ appearing after $s$ that is on $P$. By maximality of
  $s$ it must be outside of $vPw$, providing an $s$-$t$ path $Q$
  such that either $v\in sPt$ or $w\in sPt$. But then, $P$ can be
  replaced by $PsQtP$ giving a path with lower measure $\mu$
  as $\mathcal{C}_C^{PsQtP}$ contains $v$ or $w$ on top of all vertices of
  $\mathcal{C}_C^P$. This is a contradiction.
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics{u_accessible_c-x-y-z.pdf}
  \end{center}

  The fact that all inner vertices of $P$ are $C\cup P$-connected to
  $C-x-y-z$ has the following implication: components of $G-P-y$ that
  are incident to $y$ are incident to at most two vertices of $P$ and
  those are consecutive in $P$. Indeed if such a component could join
  two non-consecutive vertices $s$ and $t$ of $P$ in a
  $C\cup P$-path $Q$ not intersecting $\mathcal{C}_C^P$, then
  $PsQtP$ would give a better path than $P$ w.r.t the measure $\mu$.
  Said otherwise, we have proven that $G$ has the following shape:
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics{final_form.pdf}
  \end{center}
  i.e. it is the parallel composition of an edge subgraph of a web
  (made of the green triangular shapes) with frame $zyxP$ with a graph
  (the orange area above the triangular shapes) with cycle $PzCx$
  along $P$. We easily prove that the latter is maximally crossless
  for $PzCx$ using the maximality of $G$, conclude that it is a web
  and by parallel composition with the subgraph of a web, that $G$ is
  an edge subgraph of a web by
  Proposition~\ref{prop:web_stability}. By maximality of $G$ and
  Lemma~\ref{lem:web_are_edge_maximal}, $G$ actually is a web.
\end{proof}

\section{Solving the two disjoint paths problem}
\label{sec:algorithm}

Let us summarize the argument from the previous proof.  Given a graph
which is maximally crossless for a cycle $C$, we consider an induced
$C$-path $P$ between non-consecutive vertices of $C$. If $P$ does not
separate $C$ then $C$ is crossed in $G$. Otherwise, in $G-P$, $C$ is
divided into two paths $P_1$ and $P_2$ corresponding to two components
$V_1$ and $V_2$ of $G-P$; up to some assumptions on $P$, the graphs
$G[V_1\cup P]$ and $G[V_2\cup P]$ are subinstances on which we apply
the induction hypothesis.

We now turn this inductive argument into a recursive algorithm for
finding crossings. While we could use a minimality assumption on the
separating path in the proof in Section~\ref{sec:proof_theomain}, this
is not possible to get an efficient algorithm, and the difficulty is
to find a separating path with good enough properties.

Let $G$ be a graph with a tuple $T$ of distinct vertices.  A \emph{web
  completion} is a set $F$ of edges such that $G+F$ is a web with
frame $T$. By Theorem~\ref{theo:main_2} such a web completion exists
iff $T$ is crossless; thus we generalize and strenghten the two
disjoint paths problem as follows:

\medskip%
\noindent\textsc{Two Disjoint Paths or Web Completion}\\
\noindent\textbf{Input:} A graph with a tuple of distinct vertices.\\
\noindent\textbf{Output:} A crossing or a web completion.%
\medskip%

In the next two sections we only consider the decision version of this
problem. We discuss the actual computation of crossings and web
completions in
Section~\ref{sec:computing_crossings_and_web_completions}, and
algorithmic complexity in
Section~\ref{sec:complexity}.

\subsection{General method}

A set of edges $F$ is \emph{safe} when $T$ is crossed in $G$ whenever it
is crossed in $G+F$. Note that if $T$ is crossed then all sets of
edges are safe. As observed previously, edges of the form $x_ix_{i+1}$
or $x_kx_1$ are safe for $T=x_1,\dots, x_k$, so that we can
assume w.l.o.g, that $T$ induces a cycle $C$ in $G$.

The goal is to devise a divide-and-conquer strategy whose recursive
case can be outlined as follows: given a graph $G$ with a cycle $C$,
find two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ with cycles $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
\item $G$ is the parallel composition of $G_1$ with $G_2$,
  and
\item $C$ is crossed in $G$ iff $C_1$ or $C_2$ is crossed,
  respectively in $G_1$ and $G_2$.
\end{itemize}
There are two base cases: 1/ if all $C$-paths of $G$ are between consecutive vertices of $C$ then
$C$ is crossless; and 2/ given a $C$-path $P$ between non-consecutive vertices of $C$, if $C-P$ is $P$-connected, then $C$ is crossed in $G$.
\begin{proposition}
  \label{prop:subinstances}
  Let $P$ be a $C$-path of $G$ and $P_1,P_2$ be the two distinct
  subpaths of $C$ sharing their ends with $P$ and such that
  $C=P_1\overline{P_2}$.

  If $P$ separates $P_1$ from $P_2$ then they are respectively
  contained in subgraphs $G_1$ and $G_2$ of $G$ and $G$ is the
  parallel composition of $G_1$ and $G_2$ along $P$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
  Note that $\mathring{P_1}$ and $\mathring{P_2}$ are both non-empty
  as a consequence of $P$ being a separator of $C$.

  The statement follows by looking at components of
  $G-P$. Any such component containing vertices of $\mathring{P_i}$ is
  associated to $G_i$. All other components as well as edges
  between non-consecutive vertices of $P$
  are arbitrarily distributed between $G_1$ and $G_2$. The graph $G_i$
  is defined as the subgraph of $G$ induced by the union of $P$ with
  the components of $G-P$ associated with $G_i$ to which any edge between
  non-consecutive vertices of $P$
  it is not associated with is removed. The fact that $G$ is
  indeed the parallel composition of $G_1$ and $G_2$ along $P$ follows
  easily from $P$ being a separator of $P_1$ and $P_2$.
\end{proof}

At this point we would like to use the pairs $(G_i,C_i)$ (with
$C_i=P_iP$) as subinstances. Unfortunately, in general it is false
that $C_1$ or $C_2$ is crossed (resp. in $G_1$ and $G_2$) iff $C$
is crossed in $G$. The left-hand side example of
Figure~\ref{fig:wrong_sub_instances} shows a graph $G$ given as the
parallel composition of two graphs $G_1$ and $G_2$, each corresponding
to a coloured area of the drawing (note that two edges do cross so
this is indeed a drawing and not a plane embedding). The path $P$ is
the one in the intersection of the two graphs. The cycle $C$ is the
outer $4$-cycle. The cycle $C_1$ is crossed in $G_1$ while $C$
crossless in $G$. On the right-hand side of
Figure~\ref{fig:wrong_sub_instances} we have displayed the only web
completion of $G$ (see how it can be built by adding one
clique of order $2$ on some triangle of the only rib
of order $5$ with a frame of length $4$ in Figure~\ref{fig:web_examples}).
It cannot be expressed as the parallel composition of two graphs along
$P$: somehow the wanted subinstances induced by $P$ in $G$ do not
behave well with web completions.
\begin{figure}
  \centering
  \includegraphics{wrong_sub_instances.pdf}
  \caption{A graph $G$ and its only web completion w.r.t. its outer $4$-cycle.}
  \label{fig:wrong_sub_instances}
\end{figure}

We solve this issue by ensuring some connectivity assumption on $P$.
Given $i\in\{1,2\}$, we say that a vertex $y\in P$ \emph{is on $P$-side
  $i$} when $y$ and $\mathring{P_i}$ are $P$-connected.
\begin{proposition}
  \label{prop:subinstances_P_sides}
  Let $P$ be a $C$-path of $G$ and $P_1,P_2$ be the two distinct
  subpaths of $C$ sharing their ends with $P$ and such that
  $C=P_1\overline{P_2}$.

  If $P$ separates $P_1$ from $P_2$ and all vertices of $P$ are on
  both $P$-sides, then $C$ is crossed in $G$ iff $P_1P$ or $P_2P$ is
  crossed (resp. in $G_1$ and $G_2$).
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
  Suppose that $P_1$ and $P_2$ are separated by $P$, and that all
  vertices of $P$ are on both $P$-sides. We prove
  the contrapositives of both implications.
  \begin{itemize}
  \item Assume that $P_iP$ is crossless in $G_i$ for all $i\in\{1,2\}$.
    By Theorem~\ref{theo:main_2}, $G_i$ has a web completion $F_i$.

    In $G_i+F_i$, the path $P$ must be induced. Indeed, if $xy$ were
    an edge of $G_i+F_i$ between non-consecutive vertices of $P$, then
    we could consider $z$ an inner vertex of $xPy$. As $z$ is on both
    $P$-sides, there is in $G_i$ a $\mathring{P_i}$-$z$ path
    $Q$. The pair $(Q,xy)$ is a crossing of $P_iP$ in the web
    $G_i+F_i$, a contradiction.

    By Proposition~\ref{prop:generating_webs_parallel} the web
    composition of $G_1+F_1$ with $G_2+F_2$ along $P$ is a web,
    proving that $G$ has a web completion in the form of
    $F_1\cup F_2$, and as a consequence of Theorem~\ref{theo:main_2}
    that $C$ is crossless.
  \item Suppose $C$ is crossless. Consider a component $D$ of
    $G-P$ containing vertices of neither $P_1$ nor $P_2$. It is
    incident to at most two vertices of $P$ and those must be
    consecutive. Indeed, if that was not the case then $D$ would
    induce an $x$-$y$ path $Q$ between non-consecutive vertices of
    $P$. Let $z$ be an inner vertex of $xPy$. As $z$ is on both
    $P$-sides, there are $\mathring{P_1}$ -$z$ ad
    $z$-$\mathring{P_2}$ paths $R$ and $S$ inner disjoint with $C$,
    $P$, and $Q$. The pair $(PxQyP,RS)$ is a crossing of $C$ in
    $G$, a contradiction. The same reasoning works by replacing $D$
    with an edge between non-consecutive vertices of $P$, so that $P$
    is induced in $G$.

    Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the set of all components of $G-P$ containing
    vertices of neither $P_1$ nor $P_2$. $C$ is crossless in
    $G-\mathcal{D}$, so by Theorem~\ref{theo:main_2} we let $F$ be an
    associated web completion. As edges between non-consecutive
    vertices of $P$ make $C$ be crossed, $P$ must remain induced in
    $(G-\mathcal{D})+F$. Hence $P$'s vertices are all in the rib of
    $(G-\mathcal{D})+F$. This gives webs $H_i$ with frames $P_iP$ such
    that $(G-\mathcal{D})+F$ is their web composition along $P$.
    Obviously $H_i$ is a web containing $G_i-\mathcal{D}$. For each
    component $D$ of $\mathcal{D}$ incident to, say, an edge $xy$ of
    $P$, if its vertices are in $G_i$ then we make them all into a
    clique, and adjacent to all vertices of the triangle of $H_i$'s
    rib containing $xy$ as well as to all vertices of the clique of
    this triangle.

    This construction provides a web completion of both $G_1$ and
    $G_2$ proving that $P_1$ and $P_2$ are crossless, respectively in
    $G_1P$ and $G_2P$.
  \end{itemize}
\end{proof}

The example of Figure~\ref{fig:wrong_sub_instances} proves that for
some graphs no $C$-path $P$ may be used to apply this proposition
and get two subinstances. Given a $C$-path $P$ of $G$ we call
\emph{$P$-completion} a safe set of edges $F$ such that $P+F$ contains
a $C$-path $P'$ whose vertices are all on both $P'$-sides in
$G+F$.

\begin{proposition}
  Let $G$ be a graph given with a cycle $C$. For any $C$-path $P$
  between non-consecutive vertices of $C$ there exists a
  $P$-completion.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
  Assume $P=y_1\dots y_l$. If $C$ is crossed in $G$ then $y_1y_l$
  is a $P$-completion. If instead $C$ is crossless, then by
  Theorem~\ref{theo:main_2} there is a set $F$ of edges such that
  $G+F$ is a web. Any $C$-path of $G+F$ which is induced and
  contained in $P+F$ can then be used to prove that $F$ is a
  $P$-completion.
\end{proof}

We now introduce our general method in
Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method}. We assume that a call to
$\mathbf{P\_completion}(G,C,P)$ computes a $P$-completion $F$, the
associated $C$-path $P'$, and returns the pair $(G+F,P')$. Up-to
some implementation of $\mathbf{P\_completion}$, by
Proposition~\ref{prop:subinstances_P_sides} and induction on the size of the
recursive instance the method is both correct and terminating. A
brutal computation of $P$-completions amounts to solving directly the
two disjoint paths problem. This algorithm is only of interest if
$P$-completions can be computed efficiently. This is the topic of the
next section.
\begin{algorithm}
  \caption{General method for the two disjoint paths decision problem.}
  \label{algo:general_method}
  \begin{algorithmic}[1]
    \Procedure{\normalfont\textbf{2DP}}{$G,C$}\Comment{decides if $C$ is crossed in $G$ or not}
    \If{there are no $C$-paths in $G$ between non-consecutive vertices of $C$}
    \State \textbf{return} False
    \Else
    \State $P\gets$ a $C$-path between non-consecutive vertices of $C$
    \If{$P$ does not separate $C$ in $G$}
    \State \textbf{return} True
    \Else
    \State $G,P\gets\mathbf{P\_completion}(G,C,P)$
    \State $G_i,C_i\gets$ two subinstances induced by $G$, $P$ and $C$
    \State \textbf{return} \textbf{(2DP($G_1$,$C_1$)} $\vee$ \textbf{2DP($G_2$,$C_2$))}
    \EndIf
    \EndIf
    \EndProcedure
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\subsection{Computing \texorpdfstring{$P$}-completions efficiently}

Recall that we are looking at a graph $G$ given with a cycle $C$ and a
$C$-path $P$ between non-consecutive vertices of $C$. The goal is to
compute a $P$-completion efficiently. As before we let $P_1,P_2$ be
the two distinct subpaths of $C$ with the same ends as $P$ and such
that $C=P_1\overline{P_2}$.

The basic idea to compute a $P$-completion is to look at which
$P$-sides each vertex of $P$ is on. This reveals some gaps as in the
left-hand side graph shape of Figure~\ref{fig:intuition_P_completion}.
The outer cycle is $C$, the central path with explicit vertices is $P$.
Roughly speaking, we will see that the corresponding red dotted edges
form a $P$-completion.
\begin{figure}[ht]
  \centering
  \includegraphics{computing_E.pdf}
  \caption{Intuition on how $P$-completion are computed}
  \label{fig:intuition_P_completion}
\end{figure}
The issue is that there might be components of $G-P$ intersecting
neither $\mathring{P_1}$ nor $\mathring{P_2}$. They may make it so
that adding some of the red dotted edges makes adding the others
unsafe. In the right-hand side graph of
Figure~\ref{fig:intuition_P_completion} (where $P$ is the dashed path and $C$ is the outer cycle) adding one of the red dotted
edges makes adding the other unsafe. The solution described in
Lemma~\ref{lem:computing_P_completions} will be to add red edges one
after the other, computing the next red edge at each step.

Note $P=y_1\dots y_l$. Remember that, as $P$ links non-consecutive
vertices of $C$, both $\mathring{P_1}$ and $\mathring{P_2}$ are
nonempty. As $y_1$ (resp. $y_l$) is adjacent to a vertex of both
$\mathring{P_1}$ and $\mathring{P_2}$, the vertex $y_1$ (resp. $y_l$)
is on both $P$-sides. This shows that it is possible to introduce the
largest prefix $Py$ of $P$ whose vertices are all on both $P$-sides,
as well as the first vertex $z$ of $P$ found after $y$ which is on a
given $P$-side.
\begin{lemma}
  \label{lem:computing_P_completions}
  Let $G$ be a graph with cycle $C$ and $P=y_1\dots y_l$ be a $C$-path between non-consecutive vertices of $C$. Let $P_1,P_2$ be the
  two distinct subpaths of $C$ with the same ends as $P$ and s.t.
  $C=P_1\overline{P_2}$.

  Assume that not all vertices of $P$ are on both $P$-sides. Let be
  \begin{itemize}
  \item $j$ with $1\le j< l$ the greatest index such that
    all vertices of $Py_j$ are on both $P$-sides,
  \item $r$ with $j< r\le l$ the lowest index such that $y_r$ is
    on at least one $P$-side, and,
  \item $s$ with $r\le s\le l$ the lowest index such that for any $i\in\{1,2\}$
    one of $y_r$ or $y_s$ is on $P$-side~$i$.
  \end{itemize}
  Then $y_jy_s$ is safe and all vertices of $Py_jy_s$ are on both
  $Py_jy_sP$-sides in $G+y_jy_s$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
  To prove that all vertices of $Py_jy_s$ are on both $Py_jy_sP$-sides
  in $G+y_jy_s$ we only need proving that $y_s$ is on both
  $Py_jy_sP$-sides. The rest follows by the assumption that all
  vertices of $Py_j$ are on both $P$-sides in $G$. W.l.o.g. we assume
  that $y_r$ is on $P$-side $1$ in $G$. We must have that $y_s$ is on
  $P$-side $2$ (note we may have $r=s$). These two facts provide a
  $\mathring{P_1}$-$y_r$ path $Q$ inner disjoint with $P\cup C$ and
  a $\mathring{P_2}$-$y_s$ path $R$ inner disjoint with $P\cup C$.
  The paths $R$ and $Qy_rPy_s$ prove that $y_s$ is on both
  $Py_jy_sP$-sides in $G+y_jy_s$.

  We now prove that $y_jy_s$ is safe. If $C$ is crossed in $G$ then
  it remains crossed in $G+y_jy_s$. Otherwise, $C$ is crossless in $G$
  and we prove that it is crossless in $G+y_jy_s$ too.

  By Theorem~\ref{theo:main_2}, $G$ has a web completion $F$. In
  $G+F$, we consider an induced $C$-path $P'$ extracted from
  $P+F$. We first prove four claims:
  \begin{claim}
    \label{claim:yjyr_is_safe}
    The edge $y_jy_r$ is safe in $G$.
  \end{claim}
  By contradiction assume $(Q,R)$ is a crossing of $C$ in $G+y_jy_r$.
  As $C$ is crossless in $G$, $(Q,R)$ is not a crossing of $C$ in
  $G$ and (w.l.o.g.) $Q$ contains the edge $y_jy_r$. As vertices $y_t$
  with $j<t<r$ have no $P$-sides, $\{y_j,y_r\}$ separates them from
  $C$. As $R$ has its ends on $C$ this implies that $R$ does not
  intersect $y_jPy_r$. The pair $(Qy_jPy_rQ,R)$ is a crossing of $C$
  in $G$, a contradiction.\hfill$\lhd$

  \begin{claim}
    \label{claim:side_preservation}
    If some vertex $z$ has $P$-side $i$ in $G$ then it
    has $P'$-side $i$ in $G+F$.
  \end{claim}
  Indeed, as
  $V(P')\subseteq V(P)$, a $C\cup P$-path from $z$ to
  $\mathring{P_i}$ in $G$ is a $C\cup P'$-path from $z$ to
  $\mathring{P_i}$ in $G+F$.\hfill$\lhd$

  \begin{claim}
    \label{claim:prefix}
    All vertices $y_t$ with $1\le t\le j$ are on $P'$. In particular, the prefix
    of $P'$ of length $j-1$ is exactly $Py_j$.
  \end{claim}
  If some vertex $y_t$ with $1\le t\le j$ were not on $P'$,
  then we could consider $P\cup C$-paths in $G$, $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ respectively
  from $\mathring{P_1}$ to $y_t$ and from $y_t$ to $\mathring{P_2}$.
  The pair $(Q_1Q_2,P')$ would then be a crossing of $C$ in $G+F$, a
  contradiction.

  By contradiction assume that the prefix of $P'$ of length $j-1$ is
  not $Py_j$ and let $y_a$ be the first vertex on $P'$ such that
  $P'=Py_ay_{a'}P'$ with $a'\neq a+1$. As $y_{a+1}$ is on both
  $P$-sides, we can consider $P\cup C$-paths $Q$ and $R$ respectively from
  $\mathring{P_1}$ to $y_{a+1}$ and from $y_{a+1}$ to
  $\mathring{P_2}$. The pair $(Q_1Q_2,Py_ay_{a'}P)$ is a crossing of
  $C$ in $G+F$, a contradiction.\hfill$\lhd$

  \begin{claim}
    \label{claim:j_plus_1}
    The $j+1$th vertex of $P'$ is a vertex $y_t$ with $j<t\le s$.
  \end{claim}
  By contradiction assume not. By Claim~\ref{claim:prefix}, the
  $j+1$th vertex of $P'$ must then be some $y_t$ for $t>s$. As $y_r$
  and $y_s$ are respectively on, say, $P$-sides $1$ and $2$, we can
  consider $P\cup C$-paths $Q$ and $R$ respectively from $\mathring{P_1}$
  to $y_r$ and from $\mathring{P_2}$ to $y_s$. The pair
  $(Qy_rPy_sR,Py_jy_tP)$ is then a crossing of $C$ in $G+F$, a
  contradiction.\hfill$\lhd$

  \bigskip

  Back to proving that $y_jy_s$ is safe. By
  Claim~\ref{claim:yjyr_is_safe} we can assume $r\neq s$, implying, by
  definition of $r$ and $s$, that $r$ is on exactly one $P$-side in
  $G$. W.l.o.g. assume $y_r$ is on $P$-side $1$ but not $2$ in $G$.
  This implies that $y_s$ is on $P$-side $2$ in $G$ and is the only
  such vertex among $y_{j+1},\dots,y_s$. Claims~\ref{claim:prefix}
  and~\ref{claim:j_plus_1} prove that $P'=Py_jy_ty_{t'}P'$ with
  $j<t\le s$.

  We prove safeness of $y_jy_s$ by induction on the length of $P'$. If
  $s=t$ then obviously $F$ contains $y_jy_s$ and this edge is safe.
  Assume $s-t>0$. It implies that $y_t$ is not on $P$-side $2$ in $G$.

  In $G+F$, $y_t$ and neighbours of $y_t$ that are on $P'$-side $2$ and
  on the rib of $G+F$ describe a fan graph, i.e. a path and a
  universal vertex outside of the path:
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics{fan_graph.pdf}
  \end{center}
  In this figure, the green triangles correspond to the clique vertices
  of the web $G+F$. The path of this fan graph is a $y_j$-$y_{t'}$
  path $Q$. In what follows we assume we have a plane drawing
  of $G+F$ which induces a plane embedding of its rib, and such that
  clique vertices and associated edges of a given triangle of the rib
  are restricted to the area of the plane bounded by the said
  triangle.

  Assume some inner vertex $z$ of $Q$ has $P$-side $2$ in $G$. Note
  $u$ and $v$ the predecessor and successor of $z$ on $Q$. The edge
  $y_tz$ must be in $F\backslash E(G)$. Indeed, together with a
  $P$-path from $z$ to $\mathring{P_2}$, this edge proves that $y_t$
  is on $P$-side $2$, which is a contradiction in $G$.

  We now describe a process to modify $F$ so as to remove $z$ from
  $y_t$'s neighbours. Remove $y_tz$ from $F$ as well as the edges
  between clique vertices of the triangles $uzy_t$ and $zy_tv$ of
  $G+F$'s rib linking a vertex which has no $P$-side and one on
  $P$-side $2$ in $G$. We then add the edge $uv$ and fill back the
  cliques in a compatible way with respect to the new triangles $uzv$
  and $uy_tv$. The whole process may be represented as follows:
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics{fan_graph_process.pdf}
  \end{center}
  In this figure, the grey loops are the clique vertices that have no
  $P$-sides in $G$, and the blue thick arcs the ones that have
  $P$-side $2$ in $G$. The graph obtained at the end of this process
  is a web. Its rib is induced by the same vertices as the rib of
  $G+F$. The only issue could be that $uv$ were already an edge in
  $G+F$. That cannot be as then in the drawing of $G+F$ fixed above,
  $uvy_t$ would have been a triangle of the rib while not being an
  inner face.

  We perform a case analysis depending on which $P$-sides in $G$ the
  inner vertices of $Q$ are on.

  If all inner vertices of $Q$ are on $P$-side $2$ in $G$, then after
  applying the process above $|Q|-2$ times, we get a web containing
  $G$ as well as the edge $y_jy_{t'}$, proving its safeness. In this
  web the path $P'y_jy_{t'}P'$ is smaller in length than $P'$ allowing us
  to conclude by induction hypothesis.

  Otherwise, some inner vertex of $Q$ has no $P$-side in $G$. By
  applying the process above repeatedly, we can assume that
  all inner vertices of $Q$ have no $P$-side in $G$.

  Consider $H$ the subgraph of $G+F$ induced by the vertices that are
  $C\cup P'$-connected to $y_t$, on $P'$-side $2$ in $G+F$, as
  well as on no $P$-side in $G$. All inner vertices of $Q$ are in
  $H$. This ensures that $H$ is connected.

  The first vertex of $P'$ that is adjacent to a vertex of $H$ is
  $y_j$. Indeed, if it was a vertex $y_a$ with $a<j$, then we could
  consider $P$-paths $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ in $G$ from $\mathring{P_1}$
  to $y_j$ and from $y_j$ to $\mathring{P_2}$ respectively and $R$ a
  $y_a$-$y_t$ path in $H$, and $(Q_1Q_2,Py_aRy_tP)$ would be a
  crossing of $C$ in $G+F$, a contradiction. Let $y_{t''}$ be
  the last vertex of $P'$ that is adjacent to some vertex of $H$.

  We prove that $y_jy_{t''}$ is safe by modifying $G+F$ so as to add
  this edge. In $G+F$, we remove all edges between vertices of $H$ and
  vertices of $G+F$ that are not on $P'$. Those are edges between vertices having no
  $P$-side and on $P$-side $2$ in $G$: they are all in
  $F\backslash E(G)$. Next we add the edge $y_jy_{t''}$. In the plane
  drawing of $G+F$ we do that close enough to $H$ making it clear that
  the cycle $y_jP'y_{t''}y_j$ separates vertices of $H$ from the rest
  of the graph:
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics{graph_H.pdf}
  \end{center}
  Let $G'$ be the obtained graph. It is clear that $G$ is an edge
  subgraph of $G'$. We prove that $C$ is
  crossless in $G'$. By contradiction, assume that $(R,S)$ is a crossing
  of $C$ in $G'$. One of the path, say $R$, must contain $y_jy_{t''}$.
  The path $S$ must contain some vertices of $y_jP'y_{t''}$ as
  otherwise $(Ry_jP'y_{t''}R,S)$ would be a crossing of $C$ in $G+F$.
  Let $y_a$ and $y_b$ be the first and last inner vertices of $y_jP'y_{t''}$
  apearing on $S$. As the cycle $y_jP'y_{t''}y_j$ separates $H$ from
  the rest of $G'$, and from $C$ in particular, and as the ends of $S$
  are on $C$, the path $Sy_aP'y_bS$ cannot intersect $H$. As $H$ is
  connected we may consider a $y_j$-$y_{t''}$ path $Q'$ such that
  $\mathring{Q'}$ is a path in $H$. The pair
  $(Ry_jQ'y_{t''}R,Sy_aP'y_bS)$ is a crossing of $C$ in $G+F$, a
  contradiction.

  Take a web completion of $G'$ and replace the path $P'$ by
  $P'y_jy_{t''}P'$. The latter is smaller in length than $P'$,
  allowing us to conclude by induction hypothesis.
\end{proof}

We can compute $P$-completions inductively using
Algorithm~\ref{algo:P_completion}. Its termination is ensured by the
fact that in the while loop, the length of $P$ is non-increasing while
the longest prefix $Py$ of $P$ whose vertices are all on both
$P$-sides sees its length increase by at least one at each step as a
consequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:computing_P_completions}. Its correction
is a direct consequence of this last fact.

\begin{algorithm}
  \caption{Computing $P$-completions.}
  \label{algo:P_completion}
  \begin{algorithmic}[1]
    \Procedure{\normalfont\textbf{P\_completion}}{$G,C,P$}
      \State $P_1,P_2\gets$ the two subpaths of $C$ sharing their ends with $P$ and s.t. $C=P_1\overline{P_2}$
      \State $y\gets$ first vertex of $P$
      \While{$y$ is not the last vertex of $P$}
        \State $z\gets$ first vertex of $P$ strictly after $y$ that is on some $P$-side $i$
        \State $u\gets$ first vertex of $P$ after $z$ on $P$-side $j\neq i$
        \State $G\gets G+yu$
        \State $P\gets PyuP$
        \State $y\gets$ first vertex of $P$ after $y$ whose successor is not on both $P$-sides

      \EndWhile
      \State \textbf{return} $G,P$
    \EndProcedure
  \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\subsection{On the effective computation of crossings and web completions}
\label{sec:computing_crossings_and_web_completions}

In the previous two sections we showed how to decide the
\textsc{2-Disjoint Paths and Web Completions} problem. In the
introduction we announced that the algorithm would be capable of
returning either a crossing or a web completion. In the following
we show how Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method} can be refined
so as to do that. We use the same notations $G,C,P,P_i,G_i,C_i$ as above.

In the case Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method} returns True we compute
a crossing of $C$ as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item if the $C$-path $P$ chosen in $G$ does not separate $C$ then
  we compute a $\mathring{P_1}$-$\mathring{P_2}$ path $P'$ in $G-P$
  and return $(P,P')$.
\item if some recursive call $\mathbf{2DP}(G_i,C_i)$ returned True,
  and hence a crossing $(Q,R)$ of $C_i$ in $G_i$, then its shape must fall
  in one of the five cases of Figure~\ref{fig:five_cases}. The
  solutions presented in this figure to build a crossing of $C$ in $G$
  still work here thanks to vertices of $P$ being all on both
  $P$-sides. Returning this crossing simply requires the computation
  of some $C\cup P$-paths from $Q$ or $R$ to $\mathring{P_1}$ and/or
  $\mathring{P_2}$.
\end{itemize}

In the case Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method} returns False, we compute
web completions as follows:
\begin{itemize}
\item if there are no $C$-paths in $G$ between non-consecutive
  vertices of $C$, then each component of $G-C$ is incident to either
  one or two vertices of $C$, and in the latter case the two vertices
  must be consecutive in $C$. We choose $x_0\in V(C)$ and let be
  $F=\{x_0y\mid y\in V(C),~y\neq x_0\}\cup C$. The graph $R=(V(C),F)$
  is a rib compatible with $G$. For each component of $G-C$ we choose
  a triangle of $R$ that is adjacent to it. For each triangle $T$ of
  $R$ we turn its corresponding set of components of $G-C$ into a
  clique on $T$. This provides a web completion of $G$.
\item if both calls $\mathbf{2DP}(G_i,C_i)$ returned False, and hence
  a web completion of the graph $G_i$ w.r.t. $C_i$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$,
  then their union is a web completion of $G$ w.r.t. $C$.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Complexity}
\label{sec:complexity}

To analyse the complexity of the whole algorithm, we need to be more precise about:
\begin{itemize}
\item how do we compute paths,
\item how do we decide whether a path separates $C$, and
\item how do we decide $P$-connectedness and in particular which $P$-sides
  a given vertex belongs to.
\end{itemize}

All of these can be done using a \emph{search algorithm} (e.g.
depth-~or breadth-first searches) forbidding the traversal of some
vertices $X\subseteq V(G)$. Such searches will be called
\emph{$X$-searches}.

Whereas a usual search algorithm allows one to compute the connected
components of a graph, $X$-searches allow for the
computation of components of $G-X$ as well as the subsets
of $X$ these components are incident to.

\begin{proposition}
  There is an implementation of Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method}
  that runs in $O(nm)$ time on connected graphs.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
  Let $(G,C)$ be an instance of $\mathbf{2DP}$ such that $G$ is
  connected. An $X$-search can be done in $O(m)$ assuming that the
  relation $-\in X$ is an attribute of vertices of $G$ accessible in
  constant time. Indeed, this is a simple variation of usual
  search algorithms.

  Beside the call to $\mathbf{P\_completion}(G,C,P)$ the complexity of
  one recursive call to Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method} lies in
  four lines: the two $\mathbf{if}$ statements, the first computation
  of $P$, and the computation of the two subinstances. Each can be
  done in $O(m)$ time by using either a $C$-search or a
  $P$-search.

  Hence, if $p$ is the number of recursive calls made to
  $\mathbf{2DP}$ and $K$ the complexity of all calls to
  $\mathbf{P\_completion}$, Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method} runs
  in $O(pm+K)$. Each time a new call to $\mathbf{2DP}$ is made,
  it means an instance has been divided in two subinstances by finding
  a $C$-paths $P$ separating $C$. It is not difficult to see that
  the union $\mathcal{C}$ of all cycles passed as arguments of
  $\mathbf{2DP}$ is a planar graph as, following the recursive calls,
  we start with a cycle and we add paths separating inner faces
  recursively:
  \begin{center}
    \includegraphics{recursive_c_paths.pdf}
  \end{center}
  In the figure, the outer cycle is the first cycle $C$, while inner $C$-paths are
  the recursive separating paths $P$ computed in the different calls
  of $\mathbf{2DP}$. The thinner the line the deeper the recursive
  call.

  The number $p$ of calls to $\mathbf{2DP}$ is bounded by the
  number of edges of this planar graph, meaning $p=O(n)$. Hence the
  complexity of Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method} is $O(nm+K)$.

  Finally we look at Algorithm~\ref{algo:P_completion}. It requires
  one $P$-search at the beginning to compute $P_1$ and $P_2$, as well
  as one $(C\cup P)$-search for each step of the while loop to compute
  the $P$-sides each vertex is on. The number of such searches among
  all calls to $\mathbf{P\_completion}$ in a run of $\mathbf{2DP}$ is
  bounded by the sum of $p$ with the number of edges added by
  $\mathbf{P\_completion}$. Both are bounded by the number of edges in
  $\mathcal{C}$ which is a $O(n)$. Hence, $K=O(nm)$ and the complexity
  of Algorithm~\ref{algo:general_method} is $O(nm)$.
\end{proof}

Note that in the case we want to compute crossings or web completions as
described in the previous section, the overall complexity is not
modified. We have to be careful about how to represent web completions, however.

Indeed, imagine that \emph{most} vertices of $G$ are in a component
$D$ of $G-C$ that is incident to exactly one vertex of $C$
($n=|G|=O(|D|)$). If $G-D$ is a rib, then in any web completion of
$G$, all vertices of $D$ will be in the clique of some triangle of
$G-D$. This clique contains $\Omega(|D|^2)=\Omega(n^2)$
edges. If $D$ is sparse, say it is a tree, then $G$ takes only $O(n)$
space in memory to be stored using adjacency lists while all its web
completions have $\Omega(n^2)$ edges.

To avoid this problem, instead of representing a web using adjacency
lists, we can distinguish between rib and clique vertices. The
adjacencies between rib vertices are kept in the form of adjacency
lists, while the adjacencies of clique vertices are held in the form
of the three rib vertices forming their corresponding triangle. As ribs
are planar they have $O(n)$ edges. This allows for a $O(n)$
representation of webs in memory.

title: Spanning-tree-packing protocol for conference key propagation in quantum networks
summary:
We consider a network of users connected by pairwise quantum key distribution
(QKD) links. Using these pairwise secret keys and public classical
communication, the users want to generate a common (conference) secret key at
the maximal rate. We propose an algorithm based on spanning tree packing (a
known problem in graph theory) and prove its optimality. This algorithm enables
optimal conference key generation in modern quantum networks of arbitrary
topology. Additionally, we discuss how it can guide the optimal placement of
new bipartite links in the network design.

title: Behavioral Generative Agents for Energy Operations
summary:
Accurately modeling consumer behavior in energy operations remains
challenging due to inherent uncertainties, behavioral complexities, and limited
empirical data. This paper introduces a novel approach leveraging generative
agents--artificial agents powered by large language models--to realistically
simulate customer decision-making in dynamic energy operations. We demonstrate
that these agents behave more optimally and rationally in simpler market
scenarios, while their performance becomes more variable and suboptimal as task
complexity rises. Furthermore, the agents exhibit heterogeneous customer
preferences, consistently maintaining distinct, persona-driven reasoning
patterns. Our findings highlight the potential value of integrating generative
agents into energy management simulations to improve the design and
effectiveness of energy policies and incentive programs.

title: Mining Diamonds in labeled Transition Systems
summary:
Labeled transition systems can be a great way to visualize the complex
behavior of parallel and communicating systems. However, if, during a
particular timeframe, no synchronization or communication between processes
occurs, then multiple parallel sequences of actions are able to interleave
arbitrarily, and the resulting graph quickly becomes too complex for the human
eye to understand easily. With that in mind, we propose an exact formalization
of these arbitrary interleavings, and an algorithm to find all said
interleavings in deterministic LTSs, to reduce the visual complexity of labeled
transition systems.

bib.abstract: The paper is concerned with ways in which fair concurrency can be modelled using notations for omega-regular languages --- languages containing infinite sequences, whose recognizers are modified forms of B{\"u}chi or Muller-McNaughton automata. There are characterization of these languages in terms of recursion equation sets which involve both minimal and maximal fixpoint operators. The class of $\omega$-regular languages is closed under a fair concurrency operator. A general method for proving/deciding equivalences between such languages is obtained, derived from Milner's notion of ``simulation''.

bib.abstract: Checking that a given finite state program satisfies a linear temporal logic property is suffering in many cases from a severe space and time explosion. One way to cope with this is to reduce the state graph used for model checking. We define an equivalence relation between infinite sequences, based on infinite traces such that for each equivalence class, either all or none of the sequences satisfy the checked formula. We present an algorithm for constructing a state graph that contains at least one representative sequence for each equivalence class. This allows applying existing model checking algorithms to the reduced state graph rather than on the larger full state graph of the program. It also allows model checking under fairness assumptions, and exploits these assumptions to obtain smaller state graphs. A formula rewriting technique is presented to allow coarser equivalence relation among sequences, such that less representatives are needed.

title: A Force Feedback Exoskeleton for Teleoperation Using Magnetorheological Clutches
summary:
This paper proposes an upper-limb exoskeleton teleoperation system based on
magnetorheological (MR) clutches, aiming to improve operational accuracy and
enhance the immersive experience during lunar sampling tasks. Conventional
exoskeleton teleoperation systems commonly employ active force feedback
solutions, such as servo motors, which typically suffer from high system
complexity and increased energy consumption. Furthermore, force feedback
devices utilizing motors and gear reducers generally compromise backdrivability
and pose safety risks to operators due to active force output. To address these
limitations, we propose a semi-active force feedback strategy based on MR
clutches. Dynamic magnetic field control enables precise adjustment of joint
stiffness and damping, thereby providing smooth and high-resolution force
feedback. The designed MR clutch exhibits outstanding performance across key
metrics, achieving a torque-to-mass ratio (TMR) of 93.6 Nm/kg, a
torque-to-volume ratio (TVR) of 4.05 x 10^5 Nm/m^3, and a torque-to-power ratio
(TPR) of 4.15 Nm/W. Notably, the TMR represents an improvement of approximately
246% over a representative design in prior work. Experimental results validate
the system's capability to deliver high-fidelity force feedback. Overall, the
proposed system presents a promising solution for deep-space teleoperation with
strong potential for real-world deployment in future missions.

title: ABench-Physics: Benchmarking Physical Reasoning in LLMs via High-Difficulty and Dynamic Physics Problems
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance in domains
such as mathematics and programming, yet their capabilities in physics remain
underexplored and poorly understood. Physics poses unique challenges that
demand not only precise computation but also deep conceptual understanding and
physical modeling skills. Existing benchmarks often fall short due to limited
difficulty, multiple-choice formats, and static evaluation settings that fail
to capture physical modeling ability. In this paper, we introduce
ABench-Physics, a novel benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate LLMs'
physical reasoning and generalization capabilities. ABench-Physics consists of
two components: Phy_A, a static set of 400 graduate- or Olympiad-level
problems; and Phy_B, a dynamic subset of 100 problems equipped with an
automatic variation engine to test model robustness across changing conditions.
All questions require precise numerical answers, with strict formatting and
tolerance constraints. Our evaluation of several state-of-the-art LLMs reveals
substantial performance gaps, highlighting persistent limitations in physical
reasoning, especially in generalization to dynamic variants. ABench-Physics
provides a challenging and diagnostic framework for advancing scientific
reasoning in LLMs.

title: Channel Estimation with Asynchronous Reception for User-Centric Cell-Free MIMO Systems
summary:
The user-centric, cell-free wireless network is a promising next-generation
communication system, but signal synchronization issues arise due to
distributed access points and lack of cellular structure. We propose a novel
method to recover synchronous pilot reception by introducing new pilot
sequences and a matched filter window, enabling orthogonality even with
asynchronous reception. Our approach mimics synchronous transmission by
extending training sequences. Analysis shows asynchronous reception's impact on
channel estimation, and our method significantly improves performance with a
small increase of training time overhead. Results demonstrate a 7.26 dB
reduction in normalized mean square error and 40% increase in data rate,
achieving performance levels comparable to the synchronous case.

title: A Dilation-based Seamless Multiscale Method For Elliptic Problems
summary:
Many numerical methods for multiscale differential equations require a scale
separation between the larger and the smaller scales to achieve accuracy and
computational efficiency. In the area of multiscale dynamical systems,
so-called, seamless methods have been introduced to reduce the requirement of
scale separation. We will translate these methods to numerical homogenization
problems and extend the technique to multiple dimensions. The initial step is
to prove that a one-dimensional \sepia{second-order} elliptic operator with
oscillatory coefficients can be rewritten as a multiscale dynamical system.
Inspired by this, multiscale elliptic operators in higher dimensions are
approximated by a novel approach based on local dilation, which provides a
middle ground for balancing intractability and accuracy without the need for
full resolution. The dilation operator can be further generalized to preserve
important structures by properly decomposing the coefficient field. Error
estimates are developed and promising numerical results of different examples
are included.

title: Segmentation of Ink and Parchment in Dead Sea Scroll Fragments
summary:
The discovery of the Dead Sea Scrolls over 60 years ago is widely regarded as
one of the greatest archaeological breakthroughs in modern history. Recent
study of the scrolls presents ongoing computational challenges, including
determining the provenance of fragments, clustering fragments based on their
degree of similarity, and pairing fragments that originate from the same
manuscript -- all tasks that require focusing on individual letter and fragment
shapes. This paper presents a computational method for segmenting ink and
parchment regions in multispectral images of Dead Sea Scroll fragments. Using
the newly developed Qumran Segmentation Dataset (QSD) consisting of 20
fragments, we apply multispectral thresholding to isolate ink and parchment
regions based on their unique spectral signatures. To refine segmentation
accuracy, we introduce an energy minimization technique that leverages ink
contours, which are more distinguishable from the background and less noisy
than inner ink regions. Experimental results demonstrate that this
Multispectral Thresholding and Energy Minimization (MTEM) method achieves
significant improvements over traditional binarization approaches like Otsu and
Sauvola in parchment segmentation and is successful at delineating ink borders,
in distinction from holes and background regions.

title: SCRec: A Scalable Computational Storage System with Statistical Sharding and Tensor-train Decomposition for Recommendation Models
summary:
Deep Learning Recommendation Models (DLRMs) play a crucial role in delivering
personalized content across web applications such as social networking and
video streaming. However, with improvements in performance, the parameter size
of DLRMs has grown to terabyte (TB) scales, accompanied by memory bandwidth
demands exceeding TB/s levels. Furthermore, the workload intensity within the
model varies based on the target mechanism, making it difficult to build an
optimized recommendation system. In this paper, we propose SCRec, a scalable
computational storage recommendation system that can handle TB-scale industrial
DLRMs while guaranteeing high bandwidth requirements. SCRec utilizes a software
framework that features a mixed-integer programming (MIP)-based cost model,
efficiently fetching data based on data access patterns and adaptively
configuring memory-centric and compute-centric cores. Additionally, SCRec
integrates hardware acceleration cores to enhance DLRM computations,
particularly allowing for the high-performance reconstruction of approximated
embedding vectors from extremely compressed tensor-train (TT) format. By
combining its software framework and hardware accelerators, while eliminating
data communication overhead by being implemented on a single server, SCRec
achieves substantial improvements in DLRM inference performance. It delivers up
to 55.77$\times$ speedup compared to a CPU-DRAM system with no loss in accuracy
and up to 13.35$\times$ energy efficiency gains over a multi-GPU system.
